Bukchon Hanok Village in Seoul is a residential area densely populated with traditional Hanok houses located between Gyeongbokgung Palace, Changdeokgung Palace, and Jongmyo Shrine. With a history of over 600 years, this is a village where noblemen lived during the Joseon Dynasty, and residents still live in hanoks today.
Hanoks have evolved into a form of urban housing that harmoniously combines traditional beauty with modern elements. It is a popular tourist attraction and a place to experience traditional culture, as it has a hanok gallery and workshop along with a landscape of alleys and hanok roofs.
There is also a tourist course called Bukchon's 8 Scenic Views, where you can enjoy various cultural heritage and scenery.

reviews.author: JaeHoon Bae
reviews.text:
Baeryeom House is one of Seoul's representative modern hanoks, built in the mid to late 1930s (some say in the mid 1920s). It is a modern Hanok in the shape of an 'ㅁ' shape, with a total floor area of ​​​​​96 square meters on a land area of ​​​​257 square meters, and two buildings close to the 'ㄱ' and 'ㄴ' shapes, respectively, arranged with a yard in the center that was popular in the area at the time. The building has well preserved its original appearance, and has been designated as Seoul Metropolitan Government Registered Cultural Property No. 85 in connection with Bae Ryum, a master of Korean painting.

Baeryeom House, which is currently being used as an open, experiential, and exhibition space as a public hanok in Seoul, was a private residence in the late 1930s, when it was first built, for the family of Song Tae-gwan (?~1940), who served as King Gojong's chamberlain (second rank, equivalent to today's Chief of Staff to the President). It is highly likely that Taegwan Song, who lived at the time, was the owner of this building.

Afterwards, his son Seok-ha Son (1904-1948) lived in this house. Seoknam Son Seok-ha was Korea's first folklorist and anthropologist who conducted research on Korean folklore during the Japanese colonial period. He founded the Joseon Folklore Society (1932), published the academic journal ‘Joseon Folklore’, and played a leading role in the founding of the Jindan Society (1934) and the publication of the Jindanhak Journal.

On the other hand, he accompanied Swedish naturalist Sten Bergman when he visited Joseon in 1936 and conducted research, and served as a guide to explain Joseon's folklore and culture. You can see Son Seok-ha with him in the video film recorded by Stenbergman at the time. It is possible that Stenbergmann's deep affection for Joseon folklore was partly influenced by Son Seok-ha, who helped him by his side.

He was also passionate about collecting various materials and old books containing Joseon's folklore, and is well known for finding and collecting the Samguk Yusa, known as the 'Seoknam version'. After liberation, in 1946, he established the Department of Anthropology at Seoul National University and taught lectures (abolished in 1947), and also opened the National Folk Museum, which became the prototype of the National Folk Museum.

This building suffered no major damage after the Korean War, and in 1959, the Korean painter Bae Ryum (1911-1968) resided there. Jedang Bae Ryum lived in this house from 1959 until his death in 1968. He began learning painting under Cheongjeon Lee Sang-beom in 1929, and the following year, in 1930, he was selected to participate in the Joseon Art Exhibition and began to stand out in the art world of the time.

He mainly painted landscapes based on ink and color ink, and he explored our mountains and streams and captured landscapes based on these on canvas. In 1936, his work ‘Agent’ was selected as a special selection at the Joseon Art Exhibition, and he became one of the leading artists of the time. In 1939, he held his first solo exhibition, breaking away from the art world of Cheongjeon and beginning his own independent activities. Meanwhile, in 1943, the work ‘Mountain Exhibition’ was also selected as a special selection at the Joseon Art Exhibition.

After liberation, Bae Ryeom devoted himself to establishing a new art tradition in Joseon, and the organization of the 'Joseon Art Construction Headquarters' and the 'Dangu Art Institute' were the results of such efforts. In 1947, he served as a judge for the National Art Exhibition, which replaced the Joseon Art Exhibition, and from 1953 to 1967, he served as a judge for the Korea Art Exhibition.

In addition, he served as a lecturer at the College of Fine Arts at Seoul National University and a professor at the Department of Fine Arts at Hongik University, working hard to nurture younger generations. As such, he was one of the representative figures in the art world from the late Japanese colonial period to the 1960s. At the time, this house was an important space as a place where major figures and ideas that became the foundation of modern Korean painting met and intersected.

On the other hand, even after Bae Ryum passed away in 1968, his descendants lived in this building until the 1980s. For his descendants, this building will be a precious space containing memories of growth and memories of Bae Ryum and his family.

Architecture is not only a structure, but also a space that contains the memories of the people who live with it. The two stories of Song Seok-ha, Korean folklore, loyalty, and Korean painting are contained together in this house that is neither large nor small. If you are visiting the area, I highly recommend stopping by.

Urban Hanok, created during the Japanese colonial period, was the first real estate developer in Korean history.

Changes in housing production patterns made it possible to mass-scale housing production.

In an urban hanok where the concept of Feng Shui is weakened and there is no support,

KIMA: Victoria's secret garden
2023. 05. 20 ~ 2023. 06. 30

Love Contemporary Art is holding Kima's first solo exhibition of the year, and about 20 new works will be revealed. Kima, who is working as an artist affiliated with Love Contemporary Art, is introduced to the media covering various cultural and artistic genres every time she holds a solo exhibition, breaking the gallery's record for visitor numbers and attracting the attention of many art lovers. In this exhibition, the first series called ‘Victoria’ is presented, which comprehensively presents the world of works established so far.

Victoria is the largest rabbit in the world of the artist's work, and the artist planted it on the canvas by combining the numerous Victoria beings in the world. Author Kima twisted, attached, and deconstructed linguistic elements that read differently from similar sounds, changing the vic of Victoria, the goddess of victory, to big, and named it Victoria. The rabbit empress, with eyes shining like paint smearing, wearing a fancy dress and a large shining crown, symbolizes great growth through repeated great victories, and contains the author's hope to develop without stopping.

Kima calls himself a planter and plants the artist's thoughts like seeds throughout his work. The work, which pays homage to Salvador Dali's Melting Clock and Leonardo da Vinci's composition, is imbued with the truth that the artist learned from his own experience. If you look closely at Victoria's hands, which are dressed in colorful jewelry and dresses, you will see that they are wearing work gloves, a symbol of labor. When visitors discover this irony, they naturally interpret the hidden meaning in their own way.

With Kima's touch, the gallery space is transformed into the throne room and garden of Empress Victoria Rabbit. Visitors who enter the gallery meet Empress Victoria, with sparkling eyes and an impressive protruding nose, among the red ribbons and curtains. This rabbit is the goddess of victory and the Empress herself, who has achieved great success. We hope that all of you who are invited to Empress Victoria's banquet will enjoy the feeling of becoming an Empress in Kima's painting garden, where nature such as flowers, trees, and animals are vibrant. - Excerpt from exhibition introduction

reviews.text:
The Bukchon mother-of-pearl lacquerware class was really fun! I made a reservation in advance on the Traji website, and reservations were available for groups of 1 to 40 or more people. The staff were friendly, explained the class method in detail, and came often to answer any questions I had.

There was a wide variety of mother-of-pearl pieces imitating nature and animal shapes. Surprisingly, all the mother-of-pearl pieces were pre-cut by hand by craftsmen! All you have to do is use tweezers to attach the mother-of-pearl pieces onto the object you want. The small jewelry box was nice because you could decorate 6 sides, and the mirror was simpler because you only had to decorate 1 side. You can use as many mother-of-pearl pieces as you want, and the tuition fee varies depending on the type of object being decorated. It takes about 1 to 2 hours on average to complete. If you want a glossy finish from the factory, we recommend waiting an additional week to receive the finished product or using our express delivery service within Seoul. The completed work will become a great souvenir from your trip to Korea.

You can also purchase finished products made by artisans. When you come to Bukchon, take some extra time to look at some of the special handicrafts. Highly recommended!
